📌 Token Approvals: Why an Old "Approve" Can Drain Your Wallet Today

Main Points
⏺ Many dApps ask for permission to spend your tokens before you swap or deposit
⏺ By default, that permission is often unlimited and never expires
⏺ This post explains why old approvals are risky and how to clean them up



1️⃣ Core Idea — An approval lets a smart contract move a specific token from your wallet without asking you again.
2️⃣ Why Unlimited — Apps request "infinite" allowances so you don't pay gas for a new approval every time you trade.
3️⃣ Example — You approved a DEX a year ago. The contract gets exploited today, and the attacker uses your old approval to pull your tokens.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Phishing sites often ask for an approval instead of a transfer, because many users don't read what they sign.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Approve only the amount you need, review your allowances regularly with a revoke tool, and remove the ones you no longer use.
Final Thoughts

Your wallet balance is only as safe as the permissions you've handed out. A few minutes of cleanup can close doors you forgot were open.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
